content:
Arthritis pain often feels worse at night because you are still, tired and less distracted. A regular wind-down routine, gentle movement in the evening, warmth on stiff joints, supportive pillows and taking your usual pain relief as your GP or pharmacist advises can all help. In later life, the night is also when falls happen, so light the route to the toilet, sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before you stand, and be cautious with sleeping tablets, which can make you unsteady. New night pain that wakes you every night, or night pain with weight loss, fever or a hot, swollen joint, needs checking by your GP. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is for older people whose arthritis pain is worse at night or keeps waking them, and for the family who support them. It focuses on safer nights in later life. For general sleep tips, see how to sleep better with arthritis. For more on managing pain in bed, see night pain management.

Why arthritis pain can feel worse at night

Many people notice their joints ache more in the evening and at night. There are a few common reasons:

  • Joints stiffen when you stay still for hours, so turning over or getting up can hurt.
  • With fewer distractions, pain can feel louder, and worry about not sleeping makes it harder to relax.
  • A busy day can lead to more aching later. See our guide to pacing housework if chores leave you sore at bedtime.
  • Pain relief taken in the morning may have worn off by the small hours.
  • In inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, stiffness and pain can be worse in the early morning.

Poor sleep and pain feed each other. Pain makes it harder to sleep, and poor sleep can make pain harder to cope with the next day. Breaking that cycle is worth the effort.

An evening routine that helps

The NHS advises a regular bedtime routine and getting up at the same time each day. For painful joints, these steps can also help:

  • Gentle movement in the evening. A few minutes of gentle stretches or a short walk around the house can ease stiffness before bed. Avoid hard exercise late in the evening.
  • Warmth. A warm (not hot) bath or shower, or a wrapped heat pack on a stiff joint for a short time, can relax muscles. Never go to sleep with a heat pack or hot water bottle against your skin. See heat and cold safety if you have thin skin or numbness.
  • Wind down. Dim the lights, put screens away and do something calm, such as reading, listening to the radio or a relaxation exercise.
  • Cut down on caffeine and alcohol later in the day. Alcohol may help you fall asleep but makes sleep lighter and can mean more trips to the toilet.
  • Pain relief timing. Ask your GP or pharmacist whether the timing of your usual pain relief could be changed to cover the night better. Do not take extra doses or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

Getting comfortable in bed

  • Use pillows to support painful joints. A pillow between the knees can ease hip and knee pain when lying on your side, and one under the knees can help when lying on your back. See sleep positions for joint pain.
  • A mattress that is supportive but not too hard suits most people. See our mattress guide before you buy.
  • A lightweight duvet is easier to move under than heavy blankets.
  • If getting in and out of bed or turning over is a struggle, a bed lever or raising the bed may help. An occupational therapist can advise, and our guide to bed mobility with hip osteoarthritis has more ideas.

If you cannot sleep

If you have been lying awake for a while, the NHS suggests getting up and doing something relaxing until you feel sleepy, then going back to bed. Lying in bed worrying about sleep usually makes it harder. If you do get up, follow the safety steps below.

The NHS says insomnia that lasts for 3 months or longer is long-term insomnia, and that long-term pain can be one of the causes. If changing your habits has not helped, see your GP. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is often the first treatment offered, and it can work well alongside pain management. Talking therapies can also help if low mood or worry is keeping you awake. See talking therapies for pain in later life.

Getting up at night safely

Getting up in the night when you are sleepy, stiff and in the dark is one of the most common times for older people to fall.

  • Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before you stand, and stand for a moment before you walk. This gives your blood pressure time to settle and your joints time to loosen.
  • Keep the route to the toilet clear and lit, such as with plug-in night lights or a lamp you can reach from bed.
  • Keep your walking aid, glasses and well-fitting slippers within reach.
  • If you get up often to pass urine, see our guide to night-time toilet trips, and mention it to your GP.
  • If you live alone, keep a phone or personal alarm by the bed. See our falls plan for living alone.

Be careful with sleeping tablets

Sleeping tablets can seem like an easy answer, but in later life they can cause drowsiness the next day, confusion and unsteadiness, which raises the chance of a fall. The NHS says pharmacy sleep aids are only for short-term use and that you should check with a doctor or pharmacist before using them. Prescribed sleeping tablets, such as zopiclone, are usually only for a short time too.

  • Ask your GP or pharmacist to review your medicines if you are taking anything to help you sleep, or anything that makes you drowsy. See sleeping tablets and falls.
  • Do not stop a sleeping tablet you have taken for a long time suddenly. Talk to your GP first.
  • Do not mix sleeping tablets with alcohol.

When night pain needs checking

Most night pain from arthritis is not dangerous, but some patterns should be checked. See your GP if you have:

  • new pain that wakes you every night, or pain that is there even when you are lying still
  • night pain with unexplained weight loss, night sweats or feeling generally unwell
  • new back pain at night, especially if you have had cancer or have osteoporosis, or after a fall
  • loud snoring with pauses in breathing or very sleepy days. See sleep apnoea and arthritis.

For urgent advice, use NHS 111. Call 999 or go to A&E if you have a hot, swollen, very painful joint and feel feverish or unwell, chest pain, sudden weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control with back pain.

For carers and family

  • Help set up the bedroom: lighting, a clear route and items within reach.
  • If you share a bed or room, agree how the person can wake you if they need help.
  • Notice if the person is very drowsy in the day, confused or unsteady, and mention it to their GP or pharmacist.

Common questions

Why are my joints worse at night?

Stillness, tiredness, fewer distractions and pain relief wearing off can all make arthritis pain feel worse at night.

Is it safe to take sleeping tablets with arthritis?

Only as advised by your doctor or pharmacist, and usually only for a short time. In later life they can make falls more likely.

When should I worry about pain at night?

See your GP if night pain is new and wakes you every night, or comes with weight loss, fever or a hot, swollen joint.
